answer.rationale: Finance has mandated an 18% cost cut this cycle, and the incumbent has already refused to reopen price. Renewing the incumbent (memory c1) would preserve integration stability but cannot meet the mandate. The low-cost vendor’s quoted price meets the 18% reduction on its own (memory c2 confirms that vendor cut unit cost sharply last year with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing), so switching primary supply is the only single move that achieves the primary cost objective without widening the supplier base. A small, guarded switch is appropriate because the line is running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, but switching is lower risk than adding a second source within 14 days, which would split volume and pressure an already tight line. Renegotiating terms (memory c4) is blocked because the incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle. Deferring (memory c5) does not meet the finance mandate. Adding a second source (memory c3) is valuable as insurance but consumes the single decision slot and does not by itself hit the 18% target. So: verify c1 (to confirm the incumbent renewal really cannot meet the mandate) and c2 (to confirm the low-cost vendor’s onboarding and invoicing track record before committing the primary line to them), then switch primary vendor on a small guarded scale to protect the no-buffer production line while still capturing the mandated savings.
